subject: Cooking
title: Coffee Roasting: The Maillard Magic
description: A 60-second lesson on Coffee Roasting: The Maillard Magic.

hook.text: Green coffee beans smell like grass. Roasted beans contain over 1,000 flavor compounds. Roasting creates everything.

buildup.text: At 300°F, the Maillard reaction begins — amino acids and sugars combine to create brown pigments and complex aromas.

discovery.text: At 400°F, 'first crack' occurs — beans physically pop as internal steam pressure ruptures cell walls.

twist.text: Light roasts have more caffeine and acidity than dark roasts — the longer you roast, the more caffeine burns off.

climax.text: Third-wave roasters roast lighter to preserve origin flavors — a reversal of Starbucks' dark-roast dominance.

punchline.text: A green bean becomes 1,000 flavors. All it needs is heat and time.

quiz.question: Which has more caffeine — light roast or dark roast coffee?

details.summary: Coffee roasting transforms green, grassy beans into complex aromatic powerhouses through Maillard reactions and caramelization above 300°F. Over 800 volatile compounds develop during roasting — more than wine.
details.whyItMatters: Roasting is the moment raw agriculture becomes the flavor we recognize as coffee. Understanding roast levels helps consumers match their preferences to the right roast rather than assuming darker is stronger.
takeaways: Over 800 volatile compounds develop during coffee roasting
Light roasts preserve bean origin flavor; dark roasts show roast character
Maillard reactions and caramelization drive all flavor development

faq.question: Does darker roast mean stronger coffee?
faq.answer: No. Dark roast tastes more intense and bitter but actually has slightly less caffeine per bean because roasting destroys some. Light roasts have more caffeine and more nuanced, complex flavors from the bean's origin. 'Strong' usually refers to brew concentration, not roast level.

faq.question: What happens chemically during coffee roasting?
faq.answer: Above 300°F, sugars and amino acids undergo Maillard reactions producing browning and hundreds of flavor compounds. Caramelization breaks down sugars. Organic acids shift. First crack occurs around 385°F as steam escapes.
